speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) a question regarding the fire at Tofino and censorship-monitoring over government telephone lines-of information coming out of that village. In reply he said there was no censorship of any kind.
I have received information today by wire from Vancouver island which states: "Censorship by R.C.A.F. on west coast became worse today instead of better." Contrary to denials and apologies "a tight veil of secrecy is still maintained". Airmen are confined to barracks, I am informed, and civilians are forbidden to approach the area of the fire. Civilians of Tofino have been instructed by the R.C.A.F. to give out no information and to maintain a strict silence.
The government telephone operator is reported as claiming that she had been instructed that she was to allow no information about the fire to pass through her office at Tofino. However, the divisional superintendent at Vancouver did apologize, I am informed, for the monitoring and said that "he was sorry it had happened". In view of the above it would seem that the minister was not fully informed of all circumstances when he made his answer yesterday that there was no censorship of any kind. I would request that the matter be further investigated so that this house may be fully informed.

speechtext:
I should like to direct two questions
Inquiries of the Ministry to the Minister of National Defence of which I have given him notice. Second, are Centurion tanks being obtained to replace the present equipment of the Lord Strath-cona's Horse in Korea?

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO TANK REPLACEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the first question I can say that during relatively static periods on any battlefront ammunition is rationed in the sense that guns of all types are allowed a certain number of rounds per day. That is so that they can build up stocks either to meet an attack or, as in this case, to meet the possible contingency of an ultimate armistice. We certainly are not going to give the number of rounds per day that are to be fired by any Canadian artillery until they have been fired. The hon. member knows very well indeed that it would be highly improper to do so even if it referred only to the Canadian forces. But in this case our ammunition is supplied from United States sources. We are on the United States supply line and get precisely the same treatment as the Americans get. I am sure that the American military authorities in the United Nations would be the first to refuse this information.
With regard to the second question, may I say that we are always considering possible developments in matters of equipment. The question of possible change from the Sherman tank which we are using in Korea is continuing to receive consideration.

Not many months will pass until, no doubt, Canada is again locked in the struggle of a general election campaign. It is that fact which prompts me to make a few comments about certain questionable practices that appear to be taking root in the political campaigning in this country. What I have to say at this moment, Mr. Speaker, depends to quite a large degree upon the accuracy of

reports that I have seen. If those reports are not true, I will certainly stand corrected because it is not my desire to hurt any person or to heap any injustice upon him.
During the week of November 11 in the by-elections in British Columbia, the leader of the C.C.F. sank into what I think is a vile type of campaigning which people generally despise and which they sincerely hope will not become a common practice in this country. He introduced what to my mind was a type of politics which might be acceptable in some countries that have got right down into the gutter, but that type certainly should have no further place than it has had in Canada.

. . . the social credit movement through its leader, Solon Low, has displayed anti-semitism and racial discrimination.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in his lengthy speech yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) indicated considerable comfort in what he and quite a number of witnesses he produced thought was the solid strength and vitality of Canada. I believe that the Prime Minister was sincere in what he said. I would not accuse him of insincerity, and I would not want to take away from him, nor try to minimize, any credit that is coming to him for what part he and his government may have played in bringing Canada to the position of one of the leading countries of the world. But while I grant his sincerity, I cannot agree with him in all that he said, that all is as well as he implied. There are a good many things that appear to have escaped the Prime Minister's attention.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members and cabinet ministers, it is a great thrill to an Irishman to see a good battle, even though it has not gone farther than a verbal contest. I congratulate both leaders of the groups in the corner of the chamber on the fight they are putting up. I almost thought I was in British Columbia.
May I extend my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I thought they did a good job, and noted that they did not forget their own constituencies.
I do not know whom to thank for the honour of being permitted to sit beside a wearer of the Victoria Cross, but I esteem it a high honour indeed. As I think of these two members who wear the Victoria Cross, I pause to wonder at our good fortune that they have been spared to come to us on this side of the river Jordan.
I make this special reference because I wish particularly to congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), as well as his deputy minister, Dr. Arthur MacNamara, upon the work they did recently. It will be recalled that Dr. MacNamara was appointed conciliator in a serious strike at the lakehead, one which affected not only the workers and the elevator owners but also the farmers of western Canada. He did an outstanding job for both sides, and there was no strike. That is the kind of work we like our government departments to do.
This brings me to the statement of my belief, that the time is due when strikes should be obliterated. But they will not be

The Address-Mr. Mclvor wiped out until something better is put in their place. We should be able to suggest what it should be. My suggestion would be that industry and business concerns should give their workers fair salaries and a share of the profits. Where this has been tried it has worked effectively, not only to the advantage of the workers but also to the advantage of the government in the receipt of greater taxes, and to that of the industries concerned through higher income.
I have here a letter which deals with the Lincoln Electric Company of Cleveland, Ohio, showing that in that organization the salaries of the workers almost doubled, and that at the same time the company's income doubled, with a resulting increased taxation to the government.
This is the cure for strikes; and when we have men in business, as we have today in Fort William, who are prepared to give this scheme a try, there is hope that strikes will be a thing of the past.
Strikes are like wars in that they are a form of coercion. A strike or a shut-down is simply a use of force, and does not result in good relations between workers and management. Directors of companies would be well advised to consider a situation in which workers and management would share in the profits.
Turning to the speech from the throne, let me say I was one of those who stood in the Senate chamber behind Mr. Speaker for about forty-five minutes when the speech from the throne was delivered in that chamber. Is there any cure? I suggest that the cure would be to have the speech delivered in one language only. I do not think a speech from the throne is any more important than our time of worship in this house. His Excellency the Governor General through the speech from the throne delivers a message from the government to the Senate and to hon. members of this house while our Speaker addresses the King of Kings. If our prayers are delivered in just the one language, why could not the speech from the throne be delivered in English one year and in French the next.
I should like to say a word about the government. I realize that I sit on this side of the house and if I did not agree with the government I would have no business being here. This government has done an outstanding job by having been in power since 1935, during the course of one war and the preparations for another, without there being one accusation of graft in the speeches yesterday. I think the President of the United States should be sending scouts to this country to find out how this government has been
IMr. Mclvor.1
able to do this. I think this is a marvellous performance considering all the contracts that have been let and the amount of money that has been spent.
There are three things in the speech from the throne with which I am greatly pleased. The first is the consideration that is being given to war veterans. I am going to suggest one thing in this connection, that a war veteran in receipt of a pension-the pension is never large-should be allowed to keep a roomer or boarder in his home. This would not hurt the government in any way; it would not take a dollar from the government, in fact it would help the government. I know that some hon. members have read in the Legion's magazine that this practice is denied to certain veterans and they are not permitted to keep boarders or roomers. If they were their small incomes would be supplemented.
I was pleased to see that retired civil servants are going to receive some consideration. I hope that consideration will also be given to the widows of civil servants and that their pensions will be increased.
As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has said, the government in carrying out public works is going to employ anybody. I suppose this means that red, white or yellow will be employed provided they do a decent day's work. They will then get a decent day's pay and be employed.
We had a serious accident at the lakehead this fall in the form of a terrible elevator explosion. With your permission I should like to read an article by T. E. Irons of 404 Kingsway, Fort William, Ontario. This man is an elevator worker with considerable experience over many years and he knows elevator work from the inside. I think this article will be a revelation to you as it was to me. It reads:
Way back in 1930 in Port Colbome, Ontario, a grain elevator owned and operated by the Canadian government exploded. The building was badly damaged and there were some workers killed. Not a great deal of significance was placed on the disaster and it was soon forgotten, at least outside of Port Colborne.
In 1944, the Aberdeen elevator at Tiffin, Ontario, exploded, causing great damage and killing six employees. Almost a thousand miles to the west, at the cities of Port Arthur and Fort William, this second explosion caused little stir, despite the fact that these two cities had the greatest concentration of grain elevators on the continent. Such disasters could not happen here. The eastern atmosphere conditions were different and the fact that corn was being handled at the time the explosions occurred was generally accepted as the cause; therefore no undue alarm was in evidence at the lakehead.
A little more than a year passed, then on August 7, 1945 the thing that couldn't happen, did happen. Saskatchewan pool elevator No. 5 in Port Arthur

exploded. The giant building was all but demolished and twenty-three men lost their lives. When the blast occurred, refuse screenings were being loaded into a lake vessel.
This catastrophe created a tremendous stir among elevator men all over the country, and it was unanimously agreed that something must be done to prevent another such disaster. The elevator was rebuilt, hundreds of thousands of dollars spent on the installation of the finest dust-collecting machinery that could be obtained, and the best engineering skill employed in an effort to eliminate the danger. They knew the culprit that had caused the destruction and loss of life. It was dust!
For the next seven years it seemed as though they had the problem licked. Then, on September the 24th of this year, without any warning disaster struck again. A few minutes after the noon checkoff for lunch, Saskatchewan pool elevator No. 4A exploded.
Six men died, one of them a member of the crew of the S.S. Bayton which was being loaded at the time with refuse screenings. The building was extensively damaged by the blast and the S.S. Bayton sustained heavy damage from the hundreds of tons of concrete that crashed on her deck. That only one man was killed aboard the boat was a miracle. Had the blast occurred just a few minutes earlier scores of men who had checked out would still have been in the building and the death toll would have been appallingly higher.
Experts from all parts will try to ferret out what caused the fatal blast, but whatever it was that set it off, the culprit is the same as in all previous cases, dust. The best of dust collecting machinery, and the skilful engineering that went into its installation, had failed! What next can be done?
It will be noted that in both of these Port Arthur elevators the explosions occurred during the shipping of refuse screenings. These screenings are just about what the name implies, refuse, and by Canadian government statute the processing of them is forbidden in Canada.
The main content of this refuse screenings is noxious weeds, dust, chaff, and straw knuckles. The danger of noxious weeds finding their way back to the farm in the processed animal feeds is the main reason for the ban, which has been clamped tightly for many decades.
Fortunately for the elevator companies the United States government has no such qualms and American processors buy up all the screenings our elevators produce. Our Canadian government experts are also concerned about the wild mustard seed content in refuse screenings, and frown upon the damage that might be done to the stomachs of livestock after eating the processed article. Livestock in the United States has been fed on it for many years without ill effect, otherwise its use would long since have been banned there also.
Proper and efficient grinding of noxious weeds destroys any tendency to germinate and, if the wild mustard content is too high, this can be reduced by blending with other components that go into the finished product.
We have men in Canada with the knowledge and skill needed to process these screenings into cattle feed and in the light of what has happened to life and property it is time for a drastic change in the present set-up.
First, the government should repeal any and all laws that forbid the processing of refuse screenings in Canada. Not next year, but now. With the green light giving the go-ahead, enough capital would soon be forthcoming to build an up-to-date processing plant at the lakehead. The cost of the two explosions that have already struck would build such a factory many times over.
The Address-Mr. Mclvor
Let us now look at what this would mean. Under present conditions grain elevators have to store refuse screenings until a vast quantity accumulates, before a vessel docks to load it. These large quantities take many hours to elevate to the shipping bins, and only those who have worked at shipping refuse screenings can know how much dust they create. The longer it takes for a shipment to be completed, the heavier the dust suspension becomes, until apparently the dust collectors cannot cope with the overload. Under normal conditions the handling of grain does not produce anything like the dust suspension that refuse screenings do, and the danger point is not even approached. Evidently, during a shipment of screenings, a danger point is reached-not always, but all too often-and a spark is all that is needed to cause an explosion.
Many things may cause such a spark. Pool 4A had magnets that picked up any stray nail or piece of metal that is often found in grain entering an elevator. Unfortunately, stones are sometimes found in the grain and a magnet would not attract these. A stone striking a steel bucket could cause a spark. Static electricity is also suspected, and the experts may come up with something on this. Grain elevating machinery travels at high speed and a steel bucket may become loosened, they sometimes do, and strike the steel casing through which it runs and cause a spark. There is also the careless smoker. And I hope that these disasters never take place through his cigarette causing a spark.
With a processing plant at the head of the lakes, no such protracted shipping would be necessary. One small bin would be all that was needed, and when enough was accumulated, it could be loaded into a box car and switched to the processing plant. This would mean that at no time would the screenings be in process of transfer for more than half an hour or thereabouts, and no great dust suspension would occur in that time.
To prevent the ordinary work of the day being delayed, the screenings could be loaded at night when no other grain is being handled and the amount of dust is at a minimum. If it should appear that the dust suspension was getting too great for safety, the screenings could be shut off and time given for the dust to clear before resuming the shipment. This shutting-down procedure would not work during the loading of a large amount into a boat because the delays would disrupt the whole day's work.
The scheme as outlined in the foregoing is a drastic departure from present methods but no change would be too drastic if it would put an end to these death-dealing explosions.
As long as we have grain elevators, we will have refuse screenings, and looking back at the havoc wrought by it, some other method of handling it safely is imperative. Elevators can be rebuilt, but lives lost cannot be replaced. Whether the suggestions contained herein are acted upon or not depends upon the government.
Mr. Speaker, men lose their lives in these explosions. No amount of dust screenings of wheat will compare with the life of an individual. Therefore, I ask for two things. I ask that these screenings be placed in a separate bin from the elevator. I ask that something be done for the men, that a commission be set up, and that this thing should be thoroughly investigated by the government in an attempt to eliminate the possibility of this ever happening again. Then we ask that the ban on screenings in Canada

The Address-Mr. Mclvor be lifted and that we be allowed to have a processing plant at the lakehead. This explosion created a terrific effect in Fort William and some people are inclined to blame the government. However, you will find that the smaller elevators, especially the elevators near where I live in West Fort William, have had no explosions because they do not allow their screenings to become piled up. It was only when they were piled up in this big elevator of the Saskatchewan pool that the least little thing would cause an explosion and away she would go. So much for the explosion.
There are those in this house who are interested in health insurance, Mr. Speaker. For two years I sat on a committee and we heard experts from all over the world- England, Sweden, New Zealand. A bill was drawn up, and I thought it was a good bill, whereby there would be a contributory pension and an individual could choose his own doctor-the Christian Scientists choosing their own practitioner. Why was it not put in force by the dominion government?

Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention one or two things Fort William needs. We need two deliveries of mail a day by our post office.

I am one of those who, when the one-a-day delivery was inaugurated, did not get their mail until the afternoon. For one who is not at home in the afternoon it is just like having the mail a day later. I think the time has come when the post office should go back to the two-a-day delivery. Surely the dominion government is not broke. The post office will pay for itself and we should have two-a-day deliveries.
We have difficulties with our Trans-Canada Air Lines service. When you find a double load lining up for the trip east or the trip west then it is time we should have a double line. This is a resolution sponsored by the Fort William city council:
That overtures be made to Trans-Canada Air Lines for an additional daily flight to the lakehead in order to relieve the present passenger space shortage experienced locally for eastbound flights to Toronto and westbound flights to the lakehead from Toronto:
We hope that the management of Trans-Canada Air Lines will take this into consideration.
We have been trying for about seventeen years to get a breakwater in front of island No. 2 and we think it is nearer now than it ever was. I could have had delegations down here to meet the minister concerned but I have not called them as yet. We think the breakwater is absolutely necessary for the protection of logs for our pulp, paper, saw mills and industrial development.
Another need is to have the Pigeon River customs office open the year round for the many people going into the lakehead. An outstanding need which I reported to the

board of transport commissioners is the need for a railway crossing at Raith, on both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National railway. In the winter the children will stand there shivering while a freight train is there, or they will crawl through the cars at the risk of their lives. We believe that this is an absolute necessity, in view of the fact that on the other side of the tracks there is a vast tourist area ready to be opened up.
Of course, we need a federal building in Fort William, but I shall not say much about that now. I wish to congratulate the ministers of the government on the splendid work they have been doing. If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) were in the house I would tell him that he and his department have done a good job in cleaning up the foot-and-mouth disease, notwithstanding the fact that some people thought they were slow. This job has been accomplished with more speed than in any other country afflicted with this disease.
I could speak of the work of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) and the work he has done in extending hospital facilities. I could speak of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and how he is looking after these big combines and bringing them to book. I could speak of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and the wonderful work he has been doing.
I should like to say a word about the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). He has been receiving outstanding honours. He has been placed in positions in which no one else has been placed up to the present time. I should like to tell the minister that a great honour awaits him on Saturday when he will be appointed by that group of athletes looking after the rugby union of Canada to give the first kick to the ball that will set the game in motion. I congratulate him on this outstanding honour.
I should like to congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) upon the great honour bestowed on him, and upon Canada, when he was chosen as president of the United Nations. We admire the minister's ability, his courtesy and his straightforward way in presenting facts. We also admire him for his personal life, clean and manly.
This brings me to something I thought I should have said last year. No one, Mr. Speaker, will accuse me of being a pious sissy, because there is no other man in the house who has had the opportunity of sobering up more intoxicated men than I have had. In fact, I once brought home the principal of a school to spend a week end. Our little girl came trotting in and out and
The Address-Mr. Courtemanche then said, "I wonder why Dad brought that man home, he is not drunk." I will say this. It has been reported to me that before our men go into our international committee meetings they have three or four drinks of something better than ginger ale. I feel that this thing should be cleaned up. Our magistrate will fine a man if he is driving an automobile or a truck after consuming one or two beers. Compare the driving of a truck with driving the machinery of the nation.
It is well known that when some men take three or four drinks they become very happy. They will agree with everything in order to have a good time. Other men who drink believe that they can fight their weight in wildcats. There are still other men who, when they have a few drinks, become temporarily very tragic. They will agree with no one. I do not wonder why the Russians do not agree with anything at the United Nations. If a man wants to drink, let him drink on his own time and at his own expense. Let him go into the committees with a clear brain, his trust in God, and let him do his duty in a way that will be a credit to the nation.
I have one other word of commendation for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The cobalt bomb at London, Saskatoon and other places is doing marvellous work. At the lakehead not long ago there was a young lady who worked for the federal resources department. She was stricken with cancer, and just before she died she requested that a cobalt bomb should come to the lakehead. Through the generosity of someone I cannot name, we expect, before the year passes, that we shall have a cobalt bomb at the lakehead.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for having been so patient with me and not calling me to order. I feel it a great honour to represent Fort William, which we think is progressive and clean, and one of the finest cities in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I, at the very beginning of my remarks, pay tribute to the memory of one who shed such lustre on politics in French Canada and who represented the constituency of Labelle in this house for a very great number of years. I refer to Henri Bourassa.
Naturally I was not privileged, as were some of those who sit here tonight, to witness the political struggle he led in the federal as well as in the provincial fields. Nevertheless I have the very great honour of being one of his successors as a representative of the constituency of Labelle in the House of Commons.

The Address-Mr. Courtemanche
In 1938, the Minister of Transport made the following statement in the house:
It is not the desire or intention of the corporation at any time to obtain a revenue of over $500,000 from commercial sources for reasons that are obvious.
But the nationalized broadcasting system has become more voracious. It is no more a lamb peacefully cropping the grass. It is a lion always claiming the biggest share, and even going so far as to claim everything.
I find in Relations of July 1947, at page 195, the following excerpt:
The C.B.C. has an increasing appetite, and this is threatening to overshadow its actual services for more widespread broadcasting and better quality radio programs. The private broadcasting organizations are, in this country, a safeguard for free speech. Public opinion must not spare them its support, even if it has to reprimand them severely, when they don't measure up to their standards and shirk their responsibilities. Public opinion must in particular assert its desire to see implemented in facts the recommendations contained in their brief.
The reference is to a brief submitted by the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, which was neither the first nor the last of its kind.
Therefore, in 1938, it was agreed that the C.B.C. would limit itself to a revenue of $500,000 derived from commercial advertising and other sources.
In 1940, two short years later, the limit had already been exceeded by $273,521.89; that is to say that the C.B.C. had derived $773,521.89 from commercial advertising. In 1945, they reached $1,639,159.97, or more than three times the amount set as a maximum. At the end of March 1948, the amount had climbed to $1,842,558.29, and at the end of March 1949, it had reached $2,217,129.91. According to the last report submitted by the C.B.C., for the period from April 1, 1951 to March 31, 1952, revenues under "Commercial Broadcasting" amounted to $2,456,431.92. In other words, we are far from the half-million limit suggested at first and we are getting further away from it every day, just as we are getting further away from the original good will of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, as the grievances voiced by the private stations seem to suggest. The C.B.C. is continuously increasing its dictatorship through a type of competition more unfair and a type of control more unjust than ever before.
It is therefore easy to imagine the spirit in which the C.B.C. received, in 1948, the
IMr. Courtemanche.]
first requests for the establishment of private television broadcasting stations. It was then evident that federal bureaucracy, that had not yet succeeded in nationalizing fully and completely radio broadcasting, was determined to set up a state monopoly in the field of television.
It was then learned that the C.B.C. would not permit private enterprise to establish television stations until it had done so itself and that it would then think about the matter. Several years ago, many private radio stations were ready to enter the field of television without asking one cent from Canadian taxpayers. But the C.B.C. flatly refused to let them do so. That is why we are enjoying television several years after our neighbours of the United States.
The royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences which proved to be so useful to the Liberals in allowing them to launch a new drive for centralization and commit further encroachments upon provincial autonomy has equally served to promote the establishment of a state monopoly or government dictatorship in the field of television.
At page 300 of their report they say:
We think the same principles of national control -those applying to radio broadcasting-should be applied to television broadcasting . . .
The commissioners make, among others, the following recommendations which may be found at page 303:
(a)	That direction and control of television broadcasting in Canada continue to be vested in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
(b)	That the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation proceed with plans for the production of television programs in French and English and for national coverage by kinescope recordings or by any other practical means.
(c)	That no private television broadcasting stations be licensed until the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has available national television programs and that all private stations be required to serve as outlets for national programs.
Mr. Speaker, I claim that the government, even if it is to give us a so-called national television network, has no right to establish in the field of television such a monopoly as that enjoyed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It is in the name of culture that efforts are now being made to change the various provinces into mere branches of the central power and it is in the name of patriotism that success is attained in creating a vicious state monopoly.

I pride myself on being as good a Canadian as any member of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and I take the liberty of saying that I am much more afraid of the atheistic propaganda of some of the lecturers who have been invited to speak over the network of the C.B.C. than of that so-called Americanism, against which, with all due deference to them, private television station owners would have protected us at least as well as the directors of the C.B.C.
Are they going to tell us now that patriotism is the exclusive possession of our higher bureaucracy? We take the liberty of thinking otherwise.
What is highly amusing to us is to hear members of the Massey commission, as well as a great number of our leaders, by the way, speaking of the necessity of keeping the C.B.C. free from political interference. Let us take a stroll through the studios of our official broadcasting service. Is it by mere accident that we never meet there with people whose anti-Liberal opinions are well-known, that we often find instead more or less official propaganda agents for Liberal policies?
Now, mind you, that is not particularly shocking. What is particularly galling to me is the fact that the directors of the C.B.C., however competent and honest they may be, are allowed to spend millions of dollars from the public treasury, millions put up by the taxpayers whose representatives are nevertheless deprived of an opportunity of exercising necessary measures of control.
Television will cost us millions of dollars taken from the small wage earner's pay envelope or even from the farmer. And yet private enterprise could have given us television more cheaply; you know that.
In the name of national culture, we prefer to establish a state monopoly, regardless of the price to be paid.
What is the use talking about freedom of information, if television-which is a medium of information-is controlled by the government or, which is worse still, by a government body.
Freedom of the press must not apply only to printed newspapers but also to the talking press, the televised press. Soon the problem of facsimile will arise; facsimile is a printed newspaper transmitted through the medium of improved radio devices. Will the C.B.C. authorize such transmission? Will the con-68108-6J
The Address-Mr. Courtemanche tents be censored? I am afraid that is the least worry of our state radio, for it knows it is always right and that we shall always bow to any of its decisions, however iniquitous and anti-democratic.
Television involves censorship, that is the intervention of the provinces to approve of or condemn the films or other shows shown on television screens. Would it be logical for a picture which has been banned on our cinema screens to be shown in our own homes? One may answer that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation watches over the moral aspect of its broadcasts, that it will see to it that no television broadcast offends our children or our adult population. These assurances are worthless, as evidenced by the past conduct of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Even if such assurances were to be taken seriously, the fact remains that under our constitution the censorship of films and shows rests with the province and not with the federal government or some federal organization.
The monopoly of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the field of television is not going to promote the development of television in this country. Nothing compares with competition as an incentive.
At its beginning, broadcasting in Canada greatly benefited from competition. The C.B.C. disposes of many millions, but it needs the incentive of competition, even of rivalry, in order to function with sufficient enthusiasm.
Let us suppose that Canada had today private television stations, controlled by some unbiased organization, which would not interfere with the running of television stations; if such were the case, not only would television progress more swiftly, but our artists would not be limited to the C.B.C. alone. Through our government's fault, Canadian musicians and actors have lost thousands and thousands of dollars, which they might otherwise have drawn from private television stations.
Last July, the Winnipeg Free Press published a series of articles which had to do with the recommendations of the Massey commission concerning radio and television. Those articles have been translated into French and published in pamphlet form. I shall now quote an excerpt from page 23:
"By its very nature, television makes you think immediately of another means to reach, to inform

The Address-Mr. Courtemanche
and to convince the public. The cost of "direct" television programs may induce operators-when and if there are any, of course-to make use of films most of the time. A link is thus immediately established between television and the national film board, a government institution. It is logical to believe that the national film board will supply most of the films shown to Canadians on C.B.C. television stations. It is expected that these bodies will be prompted by the best of intentions and will succeed in reaching an excellent standard of production. This, however, will only increase the possibilities of propaganda and strengthen the party in power.
"As soon as a government becomes active in the field of communications, it can remain in power indefinitely," warns Mr. Zechariah Chafee Jr., in his book "Governments and publicly owned communications". He goes on to say:
"Zealous administrators will always invent new ways to improve the press according to their own ideals".
Here, we must take the word "press" in its widest new meaning as it is used in the Hutchins report which we have quoted above; then the possibilities become alarming.
Neither do I hesitate to accept the conclusions of Basil Dean, whose texts published in the Calgary Herald have also been translated into French and published in pamphlet form under the title "Freedom of the airwaves". In so far as television is concerned, his conclusions are as follows:
Television in Canada, he writes, will have to be submitted to some sort of control-of course-but not to that of the C.B.C. It should be the same kind of control that is asked for radio-a purely technical control. That control should be exercised by an independent commission, similar to the board of transport commissioners; that commission should assign the radio frequencies and television wave-lengths. That is, after all, the only formal control that should exist.
"Public control must not mean state monopoly over radio and T.V. Canadians must be prudent, cautious, alert in the face of American influence but not to the point of agreeing to rigid state control as a remedy."
We read on the first pages of the report of the Massey commission a sort of dedication, in the form of a sentence quoted from St. Augustine's "The City of God":
A nation is an association of reasonable beings united in a peaceful sharing of the things they cherish; therefore, to determine the quality of a nation, you must consider what those things are.
Our people are fond of liberty. They ask that the fundamental principles of democracy be respected and they oppose all forms of totalitarianism or socialism or state monopoly, even for the sake of culture. (Text):

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment to


the amendment moved by our leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). This amendment is to be found on page 54 of Hansard of November 24, and reads:

Even after the 1945 conferences, the 1945 reports, the government has never gone to the provinces with a concrete proposal for the introduction of a national health insurance scheme.
What happened in the federal field? The Liberal party came into power in 1921. Health insurance remained where it started, buried in an omnibus resolution adopted by the national Liberal convention of 1919. Not until 1928 did the Liberal government take the most preliminary of all preliminary steps, namely the setting up of a parliamentary committee.
On May 1, 1929 the second report of this committee recommended that the department of pensions and national health be requested to initiate a comprehensive survey of the field of public health with special reference to a national health program. Three years later, in May, 1932, the dominion council of health was still urging the government to do something about that 1929 recommendation. Health insurance became a matter of some serious consideration to the Liberal government during world war II.

Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time with a great deal of pride and admiration to speak on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I wish to state at the commencement that I am not going to congratulate the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider). One reason for that is this. Approximately two years ago, although no signed documents were released, it was more or less universally agreed by the house that when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell), and the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low) had done that job, sufficient compliments had been paid. With respect to that I hold that I am justified when I make no reference whatsoever to anything other than the good work that was done by these men in moving and seconding the address. It is an anachronism that I believe we can' very well do without. I think that is agreeable to hon. members.
First of all, since I come from British Columbia, I must of necessity, for the record and because of a sense of duty, congratulate the government on the appointment of their

two new ministers, namely the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) and the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney). These two dashing cavaliers from the west have earned their spurs in parliament, and I am quite sure that all hon. members will have the same opinion of them a year from now as they hold at the present time. If I may express my view, I believe they will prove to be two of the ablest men in the cabinet of the Dominion of Canada.
Further, I should like to say that it has been customary in royal circles when a king is dead to sing "Long live the King".

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Queen.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Or the Queen for that
matter, because there is a continuity there that is never broken. In British Columbia we have a king of the Liberal party in the person of the former Minister of Fisheries. But strangely enough we have now two kings in the Liberal party in the persons of the two gentlemen whom I have just congratulated, but the old king is not dead. The old king has now become Canada's ambassador to Japan. In that regard, I believe I should also pay tribute to the government for their selection, because Mr. Mayhew, or His Excellency I suppose is the better term to use now, will, in my opinion and in the opinion of a great number of people across Canada, do a magnificent job in his official capacity in Japan. In this connection there is a subject with which I have dealt many times in parliament. It will be noticed that the government did not select someone 28 to 30 years of age to go to Japan, but rather a man of 70 or 71 years. They recognized his ability, his experience and his good common sense as the requirements which would be sufficient to permit him to do a job for the people of Canada. I am sure Canadians, and the government by which he was appointed, will recognize in him an outstanding man capable of performing a first-class job.
I wish now to make special reference to the matter of age. There are in Canada thousands upon thousands of people who cannot be recognized by the government because they have reached the age of 45 years. Surely a man should not be considered to have reached the end of his real earning capacity when he has reached the age of 45. Under our present civil service system, however, he is debarred from serving in this capacity. That is something I suggest the government should consider seriously, with a view to making an appropriate amendment. Now that we are in an age of terrific scientific development I
The Address-Mr. MacDougall see no reason why those connected with government cannot find a way whereby they can use men and women of 40 or 45 years who are experienced, who have settled down to manhood and womanhood, who are capable of doing a good job for the country, but who are debarred by what I consider is a silly set-up in the rules and regulations governing the civil service. In my opinion the sooner that wrong is rectified, in respect of these men and women, the better it will be for the people of Canada and for the service they receive from their civil servants; the better, too, will it be for the government that makes the necessary corrections.
I shall now discuss the main subjects I had in mind when considering this speech; and shall discuss, too, that which in my opinion is the real function this parliament must perform before its termination. May I now touch upon something which affects our national pride. I am sorry the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) are not in their seats. However, I see in his seat the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mutch), and I hope he will take cognizance of the observations I am about to make.
In Canada, under the administration of the Department of Veterans Affairs, we have some of the finest hospitals to be found anywhere in the world. Also under government control we have some first-class sanatoria. The last time I was in Shaugh-nessy military hospital in Vancouver an amazing thing was drawn to my attention by one of the medical men in attendance. He said to me, "Jack, why do you not raise this question? I suggest that, next time you are in Shaughnessy hospital, you should turn to your right and to your left at the main entrance so you may see the plaques on each side of that entrance". Next time I went to Shaughnessy I took particular note of what was on those plaques. As I entered, I read on one side these words, "This hospital is approved by the American college of surgeons", while on the left side I read, "This hospital is approved by the American nursing association."
I realize that in the past there may have been some justification for the wording of those plaques in military hospitals of Canada, because inspection is a costly procedure. In addition, the royal college in Canada, of which individually and collectively we may be justly proud, is a younger organization than the American college across the border. It seems to me, however, that the time has now arrived when in our military hospitals,

The Address-Mr. MacDougall and, for that matter, in our civilian hospitals, as well as in the various sanatoria across Canada, we ought to be able to put up plaques which would be superimposed on those now in place, which would say, "This hospital is approved by the royal college" and "This hospital is approved by the Canadian nurses association."
I would commend heartily any steps taken by the government to rectify a situation that in my opinion is somewhat debasing to the natural and hereditary patriotism' of Canadians, whether born as such or by adoption.
I wish now to deal briefly with the Canadian National Railways. While I do not speak by way of criticism, if there are some who would so describe what I have to say, then I trust they will accept it as constructive criticism. The Canadian National Railways ticket office in Vancouver is on Granville street, the main street in the heart of the downtown business area. As one walks into that office he is confronted naturally by those members of the personnel of the Canadian National Railways who are constantly meeting the public and selling them transportation to various parts of Canada and the world. A little farther down, and behind the same desk or bar, if one wishes to use that word, is another group of people who have no interest in making sales to the public. In the Vancouver office these persons perform functions of accounting and bookkeeping. I recall vividly that approximately a year ago in that office some new personnel were taken on, among whom was a young lady who in my opinion was both charming and attractive, and who did an excellent job in making ticket sales to the public. Inside the counter, back a distance of three or four desks, is this group of people concerned primarily with accountancy and bookkeeping. What happens is that when the office becomes crowded, customers naturally hold the view that the employees working at the far end of the room should also serve at the counter. When they do not render this service, what is the result? I have seen dozens of people walk out of the office expressing disgust at the fact that the employees at the end of the room were not in their opinion doing a proper job.
Of course that is a completely wrong interpretation to put on the situation. I suggest to the government that it might be well to draw to the attention of the managers of Canadian National Railways the advisability of having some form of partition between those serving the public and those doing accountancy or other types of work. It is not a good thing for the morale of the travelling public to have them think for one minute that personnel of the Canadian National Railways are not doing their jobs


when actually they are doing the work they are called upon to do. I should like to see the government do something about that.
On top of that, there are many people who walk out of the Canadian National Railways office in Vancouver in the belief that their business is not wanted. Then they go down to the Great Northern, which company thus obtains revenue which should go to the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific.
As I sat here waiting on the leash for the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) to complete his remarks I heard him outline what he considered was the prime responsibility of this parliament. I am not going to say that I disagree with him, but I do want to indicate what I think is the prime responsibility of this iparliament. I should like to quote from page 192 of the "Report on Foreign Affairs" for the months of April, May and June, 1952. Referring to General Eisenhower, it states:
The military situation which he had found when taking command had been fraught with danger:
"Just beyond the iron curtain in eastern Europe lay 30 divisions with their supporting squadrons of aircraft. These were only a fraction of available Soviet strength . . . they were still deployed and poised as for war."
The total forces east of the iron curtain amounted to some 60 divisions of the satellite countries and 175 Soviet line divisions, one-third of which were either mechanized or armoured, and an air force of 20,000 aircraft. They were faced in western Europe by less than 15 NATO divisions adequately trained and equipped for war, and fewer than 1,000 operational aircraft, many of which were of an obsolescent type.
I think it is a generally recognized fact that what people do not understand, they oppose. This brings me to my main point in the reference I wish to make to NATO. I am not going into the various phases of NATO because all members know them, but I read that excerpt from that report to show the potential danger to our umbrella of freedom in Canada and throughout the free world.
Of all the things that agitate the minds of the people I think taxation is the main one. No one likes to pay taxes; but if people are not aware that 36J cents of every tax dollar is being spent for national defence and the provision of an umbrella of freedom, in my opinion it is the duty of this parliament to explain that fact in understandable language to the people from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
What is my suggestion as to the means of bringing about a greater understanding of that poignant fact? I suggest that leaders of all parties in this parliament, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the Leader of the

Opposition (Mr. Drew), the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) and the leader of the Social Crediters (Mr. Low) get together and make a statement. I do not expect for one moment that they will agree on all details, but I expect and I believe the people of Canada feel that there should be a joint statement given as the voice of parliament with respect to NATO.
I am not suggesting that all the opposition leaders should agree with the government, but I do think there are fundamental facts in, connection with the establishment of NATO upon which all parties and all leaders can agree. There is the question of paying for our national defence. If the leaders of the various parties in this house cannot make the necessary financial arrangements with their parties to cover the cost of a broadcast including a three or four minute statement by each I am quite prepared to pay, not with a rubber cheque but with a stamped cheque, whatever is required to permit the leaders of the various groups to make a statement of this kind to the Canadian people.
My friends, that to me is one of the prime necessities of the twenty-first parliament of Canada. In my opinion the sooner that is done the sooner the Canadian taxpayer will realize just exactly what is happening to 36 per cent of his taxation dollar. It would be foolish or even worse if I were to ask the leaders of the various groups in this house to agree on the best method of providing stability and striking power to the personnel of our army, navy and air force operating under NATO. They may disagree as to the modus operandi, but in the final analysis the goal is clear; and surely in three minutes they can indicate that they agree on the fundamentals. Then they can come to this house and disagree on how that objective is to be attained. There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that across the length and breadth of Canada the great mass of Canadian people do not understand what our expenditures on NATO are doing for them.
I had a rather unique experience just a day or two before I left Vancouver with respect to that particular thing. I was buying myself a new hat and as I was about to walk out the door, having procured the same, one of the boys in the hat store said to me: I hope, when you go back to Ottawa, you will try to high heaven to have our tax bills cut. I said: Well, now, how are you proposing that these tax bills should be cut without in some measure jeopardizing the Canadian people's umbrella of freedom? I told him that out of every $100 of taxes $36 went for
The Address-Mr. MacDougall national defence. He said: Well, what about national health insurance? I told him that was something the government and the members of parliament in all probability would discuss at the present session but I warned him: All right, suppose you do have national health insurance-and I said I could not give the exact amount that he was going to pay for a national health insurance scheme -in round and approximate figures in my opinion the cost would be in the neighbourhood of $600 to $700 million. I said: You are asking me to cut taxes in one breath and in the same breath or a subsequent one you are asking for an additional expenditure of approximately three-quarters of a billion dollars. I said that the two things just did not add up and I also said: Remember this. Even if tomorrow a national health program is inaugurated in the Dominion of Canada and if your umbrella of freedom is shot, Uncle Joe will not pay one iota of respect to the amount of money that you, the taxpayer of Canada, have paid in order to bring about national health insurance because, I said, he will simply take over on his own terms- and how.
Before I left the store this chap said: I am glad that you gave me that explanation. He said he had no idea that, despite the heavy taxation he had complained about, the situation with respect to our umbrella of freedom would be jeopardized if we did not spend that amount of money in order to keep us free in a free world, without being taken over by the countries of the iron curtain and their satellites.
Before I sit down I want to reiterate the very necessary service that can be rendered by all political parties in Canada if they will follow the suggestion I have made

that is to agree on the fundamental details, the basic principles of NATO, and speak for the parliament of Canada; not for the government; not for the C.C.F.; not for the Social Crediters; not for the Progressive Conservatives; not for the Liberals, but on behalf of the parliament of Canada. If we can get the people of Canada to understand our great expenditures in order to keep the umbrella of freedom high, keep it virile and keep it intact, then I say to you, sir, and to my fellow members, that we in this parliament whether or not we come back will have rendered the Canadian people a terrific service. Then they will understand something about what this umbrella of freedom means to them individually and collectively from the Atlantic to the Pacific oceans.

I want to deal with a great injustice which exists under the Unemployment Insurance Act and which I believe is long overdue for correction. I am referring to the refusal of the government to pay unemployment insurance which a man or woman has standing to his or her credit when that person becomes incapacitated and is unable to continue to work.
When a man or woman becomes incapacitated, the unemployment insurance credit he or she has built up is immediately cut off. In doing this the government ignores- three important factors. First, the unemployment insurance credit which a man or woman has built up exists solely because of the contributions which have been made by that person and his or her employer. The government has made no contribution except to administer the act, and the unemployment insurance which 'that man or woman has built up belongs to them by right. Second, the unemployment insurance credit which the employer and employee have built up exists for the sole purpose of maintaining that employee if he or she is unable to find work. Third, there is no time when a man or woman needs the unemployment insurance credit they have built up quite so much as when physical disability prevents that person from working. Not only do they have to maintain themselves and their families, but they have to pay doctor and hospital bills as well.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I drew the attention of the government to this matter when speaking in this house on June 10 last, when I cited an experience of one of my constituents in dealing with the unemployment insurance commission. After building up an unemployment insurance credit of more than $900, this man lost his sight. His unemployment insurance credit was denied to him, and the unemployment insurance commission washed their hands of him completely. He notified me of this fact, and I was able to help him receive payments from his unemployment insurance credit. The payments continued for some time, but while he still had more than $500 standing to his credit, the payments were once again cut off. It appears now that this $500 credit is lost to him for all time.
Mr. Speaker, what I want to know is what is going to happen to that $500 credit? Is it going to be paid out to some other person who did not contribute toward it, or is it to be retained in the possession of the government, who also did not contribute toward it? Another thing I want to know is, who is more


entitled to that $500 credit than the man who created it by making contributions extending over several years? These are questions which the government makes no attempt to answer because -there are no answers.

The government's attitude is that of a government which believes it rules by divine right.

and outside of this House of Commons to try and make the Canadian people believe this government is spending too much, while at the same time they themselves, the Conservatives, have voted most enthusiastically the huge amount of $3J billion a year that we are spending for our national security, for the social security of our people and for the carrying charges on our national debt.
Second, only in recent months-as was said by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in this house yesterday-they themselves have proposed increases in our expenditures which, if carried out, would double the present rate of income tax. And third, throughout the years the Conservative party has always taken the stand that we never had enough men and women in our defence forces and that we were never spending enough for war purposes.
On the other hand they are attempting to make the Canadian people believe that this government, and especially and particularly our Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), has stubbornly opposed the lowering of taxes, when they very well know, or at least should know, that no minister of finance since confederation has ever lowered taxes to a greater extent than did our present minister over the years 1948, 1949 and 1950, at a time when our economy was being converted, and at a time when our economy could be converted, from a wartime basis to a peacetime basis.

Everyone should recall that in the fiscal year 1945-46, when the war ended, our total expenditures amounted to more than $5 billion. By 1949-50 that had dropped to $2-J billion. That is a 50 per cent cut. For example, a married man without dependents, and with an income of $5,000 a year, paid an income tax of $1,378 at the peak of wartime taxation as compared with only $510 in 1949-50. This was achieved by our present Minister of Finance as a result of the policy of a government which certainly does not hesitate, does not object to lowering taxes when conditions permit.
But as we all remember, then came days of anxiety, the cold war, international unrest, international tension and finally, in the summer of 1950, the outbreak of the Korean war, and with these various implications, the greatest threat we were ever confronted with to our freedom, to our security and to the security of the free nations of the world. Overnight the whole situation was completely altered.
The short period of vacationing under the shining sun in low taxation land was over.
The Address-Mr. Arsenault The dark clouds of a dreadful storm of the greatest magnitude were in sight. We were facing the grave and real danger of another world war. Would that third world war break out today or tomorrow? We did not know, and we still do not know. To meet this most serious threat to our security and to the security of the free world, we were compelled, with the other nations of the North Atlantic alliance, to undertake a rearmament program of some $2 billion a year, bringing our total expenditures up from the $2J billion of the early budget of 1950 to the $4J billion budget of April of this year.
Surely, nobody likes paying taxes. But the taxes that we are now paying is the price we ourselves have decided to pay for our own security, the security of the Canadian people; and I am deeply sorry to see the once great Conservative party taking in this house an identical stand to that taken by communist groups in other parliaments of free nations, such as France and Italy, with regard to the common defence effort of the free nations of the world against communism. The communists of France and Italy also find that their governments are stockpiling too much defence material and equipment. They also struggle for a reduction of taxes in what free countries of the world are left, at a time when the fate of the whole of humanity is being played on the poker table of the world. It is my sincere hope that the Conservatives in this house are not unconsciously playing the communist game.

But where the Canadian people find yet more comfort is in the conviction that all of that huge budget is spent in their best interests by a reliable, efficient and honest administration.
I should like to read again to the house the editorial from the Ottawa Journal of August 27, which has already been placed before hon. members by the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider). This is what the editorial says:
To the eternal credit of our public men, no man in this country today dares to rise and say, or can say with truth, that a single cent of the billions spent was diverted to a private pocket from its proper channel. For our democracy, whatever its shortcomings, that is a glory.

Does any opposition member suggest that we should cut down on the billion dollars we pay for the social security of the Canadian people? Should we cut down family allowances, or old age pensions, or veterans' allowances in order to reduce taxation? Obviously, the answer is no. Can we make a cut in that half billion dollars which goes as interest on our national debt? No, unless we have surpluses which may be used to bring down our national debt. And, fortunately enough, in using our past surpluses for the reduction of our national debt our Minister of Finance is saving the Canadian taxpayers over $5 million a month in interest.
Is there any suggestion that the $300 million that go as statutory subsidies and tax rentals to the provinces should be reduced? Finally, we are left with the $700 million required for all other government services and activities which I enumerated earlier, the total of which represents only 15 per cent of the entire budget.
These are the facts which each member of this house, whether he be on the government side or the opposition side, should have the courage to face. There is no political gain to be made in hiding the truth from the Canadian public.
The Canadian taxpayers do not believe, and will never be misled to believe that, should the Conservative party have been in power since Korea, they would not have been paying any taxes or, if any, very little taxes. The people of Canada will never be misled to believe that the Conservatives are merely a group of magicians who can give something for nothing. These are disloyal and unfair political practices which lead a political party nowhere, or keep it in the wilderness.
Our Minister of Finance, who deserves the recognition and admiration of all true Canadians for his valorous, most courageous and strenuous work in the accomplishment of his duties, has proved before that conditions permitting, he would not hesitate in slashing taxes. He did it in 1948; he did it in 1949; he did it in 1950. And he is just the right man to do it again, at the very first opportunity; that is, as soon as new, favourable, international as well as national circumstances arise which will allow the government of this country to reduce taxes without endangering the security of the Canadian people.

This is the traditional speech we hear at every session, and I think the one this year indicates quite well to the house and to the people that we are approaching a time when we may expect one of the cyclical budgets of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). It will be recalled that he promised a reduction in taxes in 1949, and within the next eighteen months we can look forward to another treat of that kind. But the people of Canada have not forgotten the taxes that have been heaped upon them since 1949 and the arbitrary way in which our taxation laws, particularly the Income Tax Act, have been enforced.
We all realize, of course, that we are living in the shadow of possible war. I do not think there is a Canadian who objects to paying taxes for the defence of Canada. What we do object to is waste and extravagance.
There is an old saying that wilful waste makes woeful want, and that is becoming very true throughout the country. We see where the Department of Defence Production has purchased within the past year almost one million dollars worth of broadloom rugs. People do not mind paying for aeroplanes, guns and other supplies for our troops, but I think the people of Canada are getting sick and tired of this arm chair army for which we are buying supplies. As I say, Canadians are prepared to make every sacrifice to prevent war; but, while the budget may be quite a distance off, I think from now on we can look for soft music.
Two things are notable in the throne speech, one for its presence and the other for its absence. One thing I should like to mention particularly is the reference to mail courier contracts. The Conservative party has long pointed out that changes were due in our rural mail service. Last fall many of the Liberal members from western Ontario took part in the debate on the postal estimates, and all mentioned the rural mail service. There are two far more vital subjects with which I wish to deal, markets and taxes. I do not believe there has ever been a time when the people of Canada were more perturbed and worried about taxes at all levels of government. I just received a statement of how the taxes collected by the township of London in my constituency are spent. Of every dollar collected by the township, 25 cents- goes to the county, 45 cents goes to the schools and the township has only 30 cents for its own purposes.
I should like to indicate how municipal taxes have gone up; and at this time I should like to commend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) for the practical approach to this problem which he indicated in the speech he delivered yesterday. The farm I am going


to give as an example is known as Weldwood farm; it is located in the township of Westminster and consists of 212 acres. In 1946 the municipal taxes on this farm were $252; in 1952 they were $750.42. Farm land is not going to be able to carry such a burden of taxation, particularly with the falling prices for agricultural products. This situation is becoming so serious that municipal authorities -all over the country are becoming quite worried. I shall say more about this matter later when I deal with the question of power. I mention it now just to show the serious -situation of our municipalities.
Yesterday my leader referred to the fact that the cost of civil -defence falls entirely upon -the municipality. In addition the municipality must pay a sa-les -tax on whatever goods it is required to buy. Should there be any amount of unemployment the municipalities will be saddled with further expense at a time when many of them will have lessened incomes.
So they are in a very serious situation. I think the seriousness of -the situation was evidenced by the remarks made by the Minister -of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in the west some time ago, but it was not evidenced in his desire to find a market for surplus farm products. His remarks were designed to find a scapegoat on whom to lay the blame. In that speech, as reported by the press, he was blaming President-elect Eisenhower, and I suppose before this session is over he will blame the late R. B. Bennett, he will blame George Drew and he will blame the Conservative party. But Canadians generally are getting wised up to that and are not going to fall for it. Canadians will not soon forget how long this party has been in power, and that year after year markets for our natural products of the farms, the fisheries and forests have slowly but surely disappeared.
Paragraph 6 of the speech from the throne has to do with the commonwealth prime ministers' conference now convening in Great Britain. I think it is-I was going to say timely-but it too is long overdue, because many sessions ago I said that the countries of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization should be able to trade together because the military alliance would not last long if those people were not able to trade with each other.
I might -also point out that if we expect Britain to buy our farm products we must also buy from them in turn. Yesterday it was pointed out how our exports have grown. True, dollar values have grown, and many strategic war materials and other scarce commodities are in great demand, but

not so the products of the forests, of the fisheries and of the farms. They have followed a very different pattern, and that economy is built on a rather false hope because, should the possibility of war diminish and the purchase of those strategic materials by other countries cease, we would certainly be in a very serious situation.
The United States glibly ignored the Geneva trade treaties when we were in a serious situation, and banned our dairy products and other products under the excuse of a defence situation. Every treaty this country has negotiated has seemed to get us into difficulty, including the international monetary fund, and we have found that through them our markets have been lost. During the time we enjoyed, and others enjoyed, the British preference we were able to market certain farm products abroad. Now the Geneva trade treaties have torn that up and here we are sitting with surpluses of many farm products and with decreased production. We could increase our food production as we did during the war so long as those who do produce or would produce are rewarded. We are again in the position of finding farmers in the community penalized for producing in abundance while we have a starving world around us. There were high sounding phrases back in the days when they wanted more food. They said "Food will win the war and preserve the peace".

I wish to compliment local 2868, united steelworkers of America, C.I.O., of Hamilton, and locals 439, 458 and 636, international union of automobile, aircraft and agricultural implement workers of America, C.I.O., representing the employees of the Massey-Harris and Cockshutt Plow companies, of Toronto, Brantford, and Woodstock for their very realistic approach to the problem of markets for Canadian farmers. It is the responsibility of the Canadian government to arrange for trade agreements with these nations. The labourers in those particular agricultural implement factories are finding that since the farmer cannot sell his products he cannot buy the products of labour and consequently these people are being let out. The Address-Mr. H. O. White

Our economic conditions remain favourable and the level of external trade is high. While the dangers of inflation have not disappeared, pressures have eased and it has been possible to suspend the operation of some of the anti-inflationary measures.

Inflation has put our prices up until we have priced ourselves out of world markets, and the government is to blame. They had control of credit and currency through the Bank of Canada. Did they exercise it? They allowed prices to go up and up, and in a sense they have approved of it. They give it their blessing. Why? Because it provided the buoyant revenues of which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) spoke so glowingly.
Coming back for a moment to taxation, I mentioned the taxes at the municipal level. People in the municipalities are able to see what has been done with their tax dollar. They have their roads, bridges and schools right under their eyes. They know what is happening. When we come to the provincial level, we see our highways and the results of many other expenditures such as the development of natural resources. They are pretty well watched. But when you come to the federal level, not only are the taxes hidden but the expenditures are well veiled, so far as possible, so that we have little to show, in comparison with the municipal and provincial levels, for what has been done with our tax dollar. As I said before, the people are thoroughly aroused over the high taxation.
I believe that a complete revision of the Income Tax Act is also long overdue. It has been added to by amendments, rulings and precedents, until even accountants do not know just where they stand. Even now men are being taxed because of their intentions. That seems ridiculous, but such is the case and it applies when assessments are being made on so-called capital gains.
Paragraph 12 of the throne speech deals with the issuance of an order of approval by the international joint commission for the development of hydroelectric power in the international section of the St. Lawrence river. I think Canadians generally welcome an opportunity to demonstrate to the world in general, and the United States in particular, that we can proceed with the St. Lawrence development on our own, both as to the seaway and as to the power development. While I am dealing with power and I have the opportunity at this time to do so, I want to say that farmers and many others view with


alarm the recent suggestion that hydro rates would have to be increased. I believe, therefore, that in our approach to this development of power we should exercise a little economy. With falling prices for agricultural products and increasing costs all along the line, as I mentioned in connection with taxes, farmers and others are not going to be able to pay increased rates.
Just last week I was in Strathroy, Ontario. A resident had received his hydro bill for $75. He said, "While I am not a farmer, I am living in the country; and where I am going to get $75 to pay this bill I do not know because I depend on the farm trade for my income, and it is slowly but surely disappearing". The same argument applies to freight rates. I see that we are going to have a meeting of the board of transport commissioners, and that will be one of the subjects on the agenda. I want to point out that increased freight rates are not only going to penalize the producer but they will also penalize the consumer. Farmers generally believe we have reached the point where we can go no further with these increases.
