Mr. Speaker, for a few minutes tonight I wish to deal with one or two problems in which I am interested. At the outset I want to congratulate the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I also wish to congratulate my good friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall) on the contribution he made this afternoon. I believe that he had good material and that his ideas were appreciated.
It would appear that too few of our Canadian citizens have the knowledge that I feel they should have in connection with this enormous defence expenditure. It gets far too little publicity. I realize that in many cases it is utterly impossible to give it the publicity it would warrant. Secrecy would bar any chance of giving out the full details. But I picked up a little clipping tonight. It refers to words used by a great Yankee, Cardinal Spellman, and this is what he said:
It is better to have strength and not need it than to need it and not have it.
I believe that is the very position we find ourselves in tonight. We are preparing for trouble should it occur. We are hoping it does not. At the same time we dare not neglect that preparation because, when we do so, we put ourselves in an extremely vulnerable position. For that reason we must continue to prepare and we must continue to spend. The public are not given the information that I feel in many cases they should have.
I have listened with great interest this last day or day and a half to the speeches by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) and the leaders of the other parties; and on so many occasions, particularly by the leader of the official opposition and by the leader of the
The Address-Mr. A. W. Stuart Social Credit group, the government has been bitterly criticized for the loss of the British markets. In fact I believe it was the leader of the Social Credit group who made this statement which appears at page 59 of yesterday's Hansard:
I wonder how long a man does have to keep pressing for the strengthening of the commonwealth and the restoration of our traditional market, that is the market the Liberals have thrown out the window . . .
If those markets have been thrown out the window I am sure it has not been done by Canadians. We are told about the loss of markets. We are told about roadblocks. Those roadblocks were not erected by Canadians, and I do not believe Canadians have any authority to take them down. We have in this country no authority to tell the people in Great Britain what they should do with their United States or Canadian dollars or with their sterling. I believe they have a perfect right to buy where they wish to buy.
I believe this country, since 1940 particularly, has made a contribution to the British Isles that does not take second place to any contribution that has been made within the commonwealth. According to the figures, we have made gifts and loans of about $6 billion. Few persons stop to realize just what $6 billion means, but it is an enormous contribution for 14 million people to make.
During the last two days I have heard bitter criticism of the market that has been built up with our friends to the south. In this debate it has been stated that 80 per cent of our foreign trade, in the way of exports, is with the United States. I cannot think of a better country to be trading with, and I wonder today if the majority of the Canadian people do not feel the same way I do about the matter. Would it be right to turn down that market for cash and sell on credit? In this country today we have an extremely high standard of living, second only perhaps to that of our neighbours to the south. If we gave our goods away or sold them on credit could we maintain that standard of living to the same extent that we could if we sold for cash?
Perhaps citizens coming from the part of the country from which I come, namely the maritime provinces, take a different view. I believe that we are more conscious of the fact that those United States markets are the very lifestream of our part of Canada. Without those markets we would be completely lost. It is true that many of the things we produce go across the border in a raw state but there is no market for that material in Canada, and a great percentage of it is of a perishable character. So far as the
94	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. A. W. Stuart maritime provinces are concerned, the only normal market for it is the United States. I often wonder what sort of position we would be in if restrictive tariffs were placed on those goods by the United States. With the small population we now have, I feel that we could still look for a great decrease should that event ever happen. We are extremely dependent upon those markets.
I want to say here that I was greatly encouraged when I picked up a newspaper a few days ago and read extracts from a speech that was made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in Detroit. I believe there is much food for thought in the suggestions he made at that time. I might also say that in my opinion it is a good Liberal speech. This is what he said:
While trade relations between Canada and the U.S. have never been better, they are capable of considerable improvement . . .
While there were no serious restrictions in the exchange of raw materials between the two countries, "can the same be said of manufactured goods and agricultural products?" asked Mr. Howe, then added:
"You know the answer to that as well as I do."
I picked up a clipping today, and I fail to understand why it ever appeared in the Globe and Mail. It is dated November 14 and is by a citizen of the city of Toronto who has returned from the United States. This is what that gentleman had to say:
I have just returned from the United States. I bought the practical limit permitted for a forty-eight hour visit. My purchases consisted of identical brand name articles of merchandise sold both in Canada and the United States.
I drove home on gasoline that cost me 27'9 cents (Canadian measure) in New Jersey, 31 cents in New York and 40 cents in Ontario-
When this oil boom came to Alberta we were all given to understand that we might expect cheaper gas and oil in this country.
I can only say that in the part of the country from which I come there has been no reduction but rather there has been an increase. This gentleman goes on to say:
-on four new 6'40 by 15 tires, price $67.16 in the States and $129.60 in Toronto.
I have put these figures on the record before with regard to the tire that is made by the identical company, one in the United States and the other in Canada. The four tires cost him $67.16 in the United States, and they were $129.60 in Toronto.
I just want to take a moment to say that in this House of Commons I have also heard a great deal of criticism with regard to the subsidization of farm products, fishery products, or whatever they might be. If ever there was a glaring example of subsidization


in any country, there it is. Subsidizing industry is the difference between the price in the United States and duty paid value in Canada. Whatever that amount is that is the subsidy. It cannot be called anything else. Sometimes I believe those of us in the maritime provinces have a better right to complain about this unjust treatment than they have in some other parts of this country.
These are the prices here as compared with the prices in the United States. This article goes on to give a name brand of glycol; that is, anti-freeze. It was $3.75 in the United States and $5.95 in Canada. Only a few days ago I noticed that representatives of one of the great Canadian corporations appeared before the tariff board in Ottawa and asked for further protection. That spread is not enough to satisfy Canadian manufacturers, and they appeared before the tariff board in Ottawa asking for greater protection.
An electric mixer bought for a gift was $12.95 in the United States; it is $30 in Canada. That is a difference of a great deal over 100 per cent. An orlon shirt was $4.95 in the United States; an equivalent nylon shirt in Canada is $10.50. These are companies that are asking this government today to bar the importation of foreign textiles, at a time when there is a difference of nearly 100 per cent in the price of the finished product.

speechtext: That is what your Liberal government which has been in office for twenty years has done for you.

speechtext: God help us if we ever have a Tory government, particularly if they follow the same course they have followed since confederation.

speechtext: What about New Brunswick?

speechtext:
He mentions an electric razor. It cost $18 in Harrison, New Jersey. The same razor, made by the same company, was quoted at $29.95 in Toronto. These are the remarks at the end of his letter:
Just why, in the light of the higher wages and salaries paid in the United States as well as the excellent profits now being reported, anyone should deprive themselves of the benefits of the obviously more efficient manufacturing and distributing methods leaves a lot to be explained.
That is signed by E. L. Patchet of Toronto.
I want to turn to one more subject along that line and deal with it briefly. Last summer we received from the Vancouver motor dealers' association a great deal of literature comparing prices of automobiles in Canada and the United States, and the different tax structures in the two countries with regard to this commodity. I was down in Connecticut for several days during the presidential election. I listened to the story and

watched the proceedings on television. As you realize, during an election campaign they come out with everything they have to offer to the public. In a radio address I heard a very prominent announcer in the United States state that the federal tax on a $2,000 car in that country was $620. The next day I got copies of two Connecticut papers in which that statement appeared. Unfortunately I have lost them, but these figures are correct. According to the literature that was sent out by the Vancouver motor dealers' association the federal taxation in the United States was $100. There is quite a difference between a tax of $100 and $620. That statement was in the United States press. I can get a copy of it. It appeared on November 3 last.
When the subject is mentioned and the great variation between the prices of automobiles in the two countries is shown, the first answer that the automobile manufacturers come up with is that it is taxation. A tax of $620 works out to about 32 per cent. That is the federal tax on an automobile in the United States. I am sure the federal tax on an automobile is not any greater in Canada. But what is the reason for this great differential in the price of the same make of car, one manufactured in Detroit and the other manufactured across the river in Windsor, or in Oshawa? I feel that Canadians have every right in the world to believe that they are being robbed. It is unfair for any company, with branches on both sides of the border, to take advantage of every bit of protection that is accorded to it.
I can see the force of a new company that is being established, perhaps with very little finances, asking for protection while trying to get on their feet, trying to manufacture. I believe they should be protected. But when you come to old established companies which are declaring dividends in the millions every year, and you find that they are still asking for protection and still charging the Canadian people 50 per cent more than they are charging United States citizens on the other side of the border, then something should be done.
I want to return for one moment to the subject I mentioned at the outset, namely the loss of British markets. I feel quite strongly on this subject. I feel that that matter has been in the hands of three very capable men, namely the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). Perhaps I would feel this way naturally, but going back over history I have found it impossible to find a better team at any time since confederation. I believe these three men have used every avenue. They have taken every advantage. They have
The Address-Mr. A. W. Stuart done everything that was humanly possible to restore and hold those British markets for Canadian goods.
We all appreciate the British markets. There is not a Canadian in this chamber, there is not a Canadian that I know of, who does not appreciate the markets that we have had in Britain over the years. I am coming out with a suggestion that perhaps has never been mentioned before in the House of Commons. If we want better marketing conditions; if we want better world conditions, we shall have to do something along these lines. Our Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance are on their way overseas tonight. The result of the meeting they are to attend will not be known for a few days. We all realize they have a big job to do, but I want to say in all sincerity that the biggest job that Canadians might sponsor today is free trade within the NATO nations, if we want to create good will and good understanding.
Go back through history and you will find, and you will be convinced immediately, that a great number of the wars we have had down through the years have developed because of tariff walls. Tariff walls have been responsible for them. As I look back at the figures I find that since 1940 the United States has contributed $87 billion to Europe and Asia. That includes, of course, the assistance they gave Russia when that country was our ally during the war. A great deal of that $87 billion has gone into Germany, Japan, and countries that were devastated during the war. They must come back in order to produce and manufacture to live as we would like to see them live. But it would seem to me that it is simply giving with one hand and taking away with the other if, after they get into a position where they can manufacture and export, we stick up a tariff wall and refuse to do business with them.
You will never have world peace, you will never create within the United Nations the feeling that should be created, so long as tariff walls stand as a barrier. There is one way and only one way a proper feeling can be created, and that is to tear the gates down in all the countries within NATO. When you do that not only will you make friends there, but some of the democratic countries outside NATO will then wish to become members. They will realize that this organization is not one that takes only a negative stand or uses them when world conditions are such that we might use them to our advantage. They will then realize that we are trying to help them not only to build up a war machine but to trade with them and to a great extent be responsible for improving their standard of living.
96	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. A. W. Stuart
I believe communism would be licked today if in this world we could just fill the stomachs. It is utterly impossible to convince people who are hungry, people who are without clothing and without shelter, that our way of life is the only way of life. I have seen some pretty desperate circumstances overseas, such as to convince me immediately that people in desperation are in the same position as a drowning man reaching for a straw-"Anything is better than what we have." So many at that stage are content to accept some ideology which at other times would seem utterly hopeless to them. But through starvation and hunger they are obliged to accept whatever is offered to them.
By creating free trade within the United Nations I believe that we in Canada could continue with the standard of living we now have. We are an exporting nation. Fourteen millions of people can never consume what they can manufacture and create. Our prosperity is based upon the amount we can export.
For that reason we are the country that should be leading the way. As was said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in Detroit, the only way we will ever obtain world peace, the only way we will ever satisfy our allies and friends, is by leading the way ourselves, throwing down the gates and taking what they have to offer. When that is done we will hear members in this House of Commons rising to their feet defending industry in their own constituencies. They will be complaining because the importation of Japanese balloons, or something else, is depriving people of their living.
We must contend with that. In this connection I should like to place on record an article I came across the other day in Time magazine, dealing with Mr. Parker of the Parker Pen Company. Parker was sent to England by his father many years ago to establish a branch of their industry in that country. The article points out that in the first year he was there he lost $100,000 through not knowing the English methods of distribution. He continued in his efforts, however, and found it wise to hire British merchandisers, until today the products of the Parker Pen Company are being advertised in thirty-one languages and last year foreign sales rose to a volume of $13,700,000, or about 40 per cent of the total sales. The article goes on to say:
While expanding abroad into 121 countries, Ken Parker did not forget his 1,900 employees at home. They have a union shop, liberal welfare benefits, and a respect for Parker's enlightened methods; never in the company's 60-year history have they
[Mr. Stuart (Charlotte) .1

called a strike. A year and a half ago, feeling that the time clock irritated employees, Parker abolished it. Tardiness and absenteeism dwindled to almost zero.
And the final paragraph of the article attributes these words to Mr. Parker:
We'll take our chances on U.S. production and merchandising savvy any time against all comers. And with the bars down in both directions, U.S. manufacturers would have access to the two billion consumers in the world, instead of only 150 million at home.
I suggest he might be described as a gentleman of vision. The Parker pen is one of the most expensive manufactured on this continent. We see many types of ball pens and pens of the traditional type but, despite the pens offered on the market, this company has built up a large volume of business, and is prepared to take on all comers. They have thrown down the bars and have said they are prepared to compete with any other man. That is the spirit that must be developed in all the NATO countries, particularly in Canada and the United States. We have to encourage others, and no better way can be found to give that encouragement than to be prepared to buy from them. We cannot have it just one way: if we want to sell to them we must buy from them. I noted that in a recent speech Dean Acheson said this:
If we and our partners in the free world are to build the kind of economic and military strength we need for our security, we must all co-operate to reduce and minimize the barriers to trade between us.
In my opinion truer words were never spoken. There is nothing we can do and nothing the United Nations can do that would go further toward the making of peace and the betterment of world conditions than to treat our friends as we would like to be treated.
The hon. member who preceded me in the debate referred to prices being paid today for farm products. Travelling to Ottawa the other day I drove through four states and made comparisons of farm prices along the way with the prices I had been obliged to pay in the little town in which I live. Malone, New York, is only about 90 miles from Ottawa. In three grocery stores in Malone bacon was selling at three pounds for a dollar and pork loin at 40 cents a pound. Yet I cannot buy bacon at three pounds for a dollar. Some hon. member may know somewhere he can get it at that price, but I cannot find it. Those are the prices they are receiving today for pork in the United States.
The Canadian product cannot go into the United States today, and one would take it for granted that, with Canadian meats barred from that market, prices would be much greater there than they are in Canada,

The Address-Mr. Catherwood
because in this country we have a surplus. But those are the prices they are receiving for pork and pork products in the United States of America.
I feel that perhaps it is not only the Canadian farmer who is beginning to feel the pinch. The hon. member who took his seat a few moments ago referred to inflation. Well, there is only one way to do away with inflation and that is to get prices down. We will never do away with it so long as prices are spiralling. They have to come down, and will have to start somewhere. My experience has been that they usually start with the primary producer. That has already taken place in the maritime provinces. The demand this year for fish and fish products is much less than it was last year, and very much less than it was two years ago. Prices are down. I feel that perhaps the primary producers are not able to meet this situation. They do not like to see the prices of raw materials being the first to come down.
Today our people are living better than ever before. There is no question about that. Prices are high in most cases, but some day there is going to be a slump. It has to start somewhere. The cost of living index has been dropping slowly during the past three or four months, but the time is coming when it must drop more rapidly. Prices must fall.
In conclusion may I say that I hope the government will give serious consideration to the lowering of tariffs. I feel that that action would be of greater benefit to Canada than it would to many other countries in the world. We are an exporting nation and we should be leading the way. If we want to create a feeling of respect, if we want to give the people of other countries hope for the future, we cannot follow a better course than to throw down our tariff walls and deal with our friends and allies as we would like to have them deal with us.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the privileges we have under our system of government is that of taking part in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I trust that this privilege will be long continued and that no effort will be made to drastically curtail a discussion which permits us to voice our grievances, to express our ideas and to bring parliament more or less up to date. I know there are those who will disagree with me on this score, but I do trust there will be no curtailment of this discussion. It is true that there is a certain amount of repetition; it is true there are some rather long speeches, but I feel that the collective views expressed in this debate give us a knowledge that is well for us to have.
We are meeting under conditions which are not greatly changed from those which obtained when we adjourned in July. Canada is still building up defences against aggression in an effort to avert global conflict. This is something close to the hearts and minds of all of us. We hope these efforts will continue, because if another global war were to develop it would create the most calamitous situation this world has ever known.
I think our people are generally in accord with the government on its defence policy provided reasonable value is obtained for the expenditures made. The question is whether we are getting value for the money spent in this regard. From the rather shocking revelations in the press and the questions that have been asked in the house it would seem to be indicated that we have not been getting full value for our defence expenditures. The references that have been made to the ultraextravagant methods pursued by the defence purchasing department has created grave doubts in our mind.
We as members of Her Majesty's most loyal opposition, and I think the majority of the 14 million people of Canada, will go all-out with the government provided our country is placed on an equal standing with other free nations in the world. We will co-operate to the full if our government provides the best of military equipment for all our armed forces. We will give credit where credit is due when the government acts as we feel it should in the best interests of all the people of Canada.
But we will not and we cannot acquiesce in expenditures of the type that have just been brought to our notice. I think it is the duty of every member of parliament to scrutinize closely every expenditure of government, not just defence expenditures. I hope the day will never come when we are not permitted to carry out this prerogative to the full. I hope the day will never come when the government of the day will not invite or even welcome all members-and not just those of the opposition-to dig deeply into the intricacies of government operations. If by so doing they are able to find inequalities, unjustifiable actions, improper methods and deficiencies the government should congratulate the members who have brought such matters to their attention and take immediate steps to remedy the situation. That is my idea of good government.
I came to parliament-and I know this is true of all hon. members-with the idea of being useful and of giving the best representation possible. The people of Haldimand, whom I have the privilege of representing, are pretty sound-thinking people. They have
98

The Address-Mr. Catherwood proved this by consistently returning Conservative members to this house for the past fifty years. You cannot continue to be associated with people such as we have in Haldi-mand-and this would apply to most rural constituencies-unless your actions and voice reflect the thinking of those people.
As their representatives in this the highest court of the land they expect us to protect their interests, to protect their rights and to protect their privileges at all times. That is our trust. It is a great honour to be a member of parliament. I hope no government member will criticize or condemn any member of this house, even a member of the government party, who makes an effort, rightly or perhaps even wrongly at times- this does not occur too often

to improve or better conditions through the medium of this House of Commons.
It is rather interesting to note how much further advanced is the National Liberal Federation than is the government itself. There was a recent meeting of the Liberal federation at which a number of resolutions were passed which were in complete conformity with views which have been expressed in the House of Commons by members of the opposition. Hon. members will recall how in recent sessions our party, under the leadership of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), so well brought to the attention of this house the great needs of many of our veterans and their families. We know something of what those needs are. Because of the high cost of living, these people were finding it difficult to get along. We now find that the National Liberal Federation is in complete agreement with the suggestions that were made in this house by the Conservative party.
Hon. members will also recall that at every session since the commencement of the twenty-first parliament we have requested the government to take some action in connection with the Post Office Department. We are glad to notice that the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) is showing an increasing interest in these matters. These problems are most serious, and they have been brought to the attention of the government on many occasions. There have been complaints about mail deliveries in the urban centres and the plight of the rural mail carriers. The National Liberal Federation has recognized again the reasonableness of the oft-repeated request made in this house by members of our party. Then again we find the Liberal congress in complete acquiescence with our views in regard to the abolition of the nuisance radio
licence fee of $2.50. That has been brought very strongly to the attention of the house by my leader and others on many occasions. We have requested that the C.B.C. should not have a monopoly on radio and television service across the country. That too was brought very forcibly to the attention of the house by my leader in his opening address in this debate, and again we find the Liberal federation approving that policy.
As we look back over the past three and one-half years we find on the pages of Hansard innumerable references by members of our party to which members of the Liberal federation now give their support. In other words they now support those things for which we have pressed for many years.
There was one particular matter I would like to bring to the attention of the government, more particularly to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham). He is not in his seat at the present time, but I would like to suggest that he undertake a geological survey in a certain section of southwestern Ontario. On this I would like to quote Mr. W. A. Bell at page 18 of the statistics for the department where he says:
The guiding objective of the geological survey is a systematic study of the geology of Canada. Until the geology of any area is thoroughly known no just appraisal can be made of the economic value of its rocks and unconsolidated deposits, and of the probabilities of the occurrence of commercial quantities of minerals and fuels.
Further on in his survey report Mr. Bell states that geological surveys have provided data of great value to the discovery and development of oil in the foothills of Alberta. We certainly have no quarrel with that statement; I think it is quite true. My reason for asking for a survey of the southwestern Ontario area is because of the immense resources of natural gas we have in that section of which Haldimand county may be classed as the centre. As the production of natural gas is associated with oil in many cases, I think it would be particularly justifiable to ask for a survey.
Haldimand county has over 2,000 natural gas wells and the neighbouring county of Norfolk has approximately 350, with a combined annual production of well over 2 billion cubic feet of gas. We also have the gas field in the southwestern portion of Ontario along the shores of lake Erie, where owing to the heavily-producing gas area oil might be found. I trust the minister will give some consideration to this request, as I feel under the conditions it is a very normal one we are making.
The Conservative party has consistently urged the government to give some measure

of relief to the taxpayers, but this request has just as consistently fallen on deaf ears. Our party has pointed out that the policies of overtaxation which have been so much in evidence since the election of 1949 have created a feeling of frustration and a feeling of "what's the use" in so many of our people. In spite of that the government has increased taxes beginning with the first budget after 1949, producing huge surpluses, and has repeatedly stated each year that they have to tax heavily in order that we may continue our defence and social security projects. I think the best answer that has been given comes from the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants and the Canadian Bar Association, an organization I know all hon. members will agree is of a non-political nature. After a most careful study of the tax structure they have concluded that a substantial measure of relief could be given. They announced that a surplus of $300 million could very well be possible; and the suggestions were made after careful study of the situation.
The Canadian people have reason to believe that this high taxation should be cut down to a certain extent, for to be overtaxed year after year just means that there are many sacrifices which have to be made by our people. For instance, they cannot make a little extra payment on a mortgage as otherwise they might. They perhaps cannot buy that fur coat-or not perhaps a fur coat but a badly needed coat for the wife-and it means giving up many other little things that go to make our way of life what so many of our Canadian people feel it should be.
There is just one other matter I would like to deal with, and it is one which is and should be of great concern to every member of this house. I refer particularly to the fact that there was no reference in the speech from the throne to the situation which concerns the farm people in this country, and the disposition of our farm products. I have just completed reading a lengthy and rather detailed account of the meeting of the United Nations food and agriculture organization held in Rome this year. After reading that report I find it emphasizes the often expressed sentiments of so many people that there is definitely something radically wrong with our system of food distribution throughout this and other lands. It is unfortunate that some system cannot be devised under which we could have a more proper distribution of food throughout the rest of the world. Each year, and perhaps this year more than at any other time, the FAO has striven to emphasize the urgent need for greater production of foods to ensure the very minimum of requirements for the people of the world.
The Address-Mr. Catherwood
I would like to ask members of this house if it is just the purpose of this organization to meet year after year to study and analyse the world food situation, to make recommendations as to what should be done, and there to let the matter rest. To many people the setting up of that organization some seven years ago was one thing in which we felt there would be an advance, something to help solve the world's greatest problem next to that of war, that of relief from the haunting fear of hunger and starvation. In many places throughout the Asiatic world people are starving due to the fact that we have not as yet established that necessary form of distribution. What hope is there for a free world as long as that situation continues, after seven years of meeting together with members of over sixty nations; and what have we accomplished? Exactly nothing. When we consider the high hopes we had at that time and what little has been attained we naturally feel that this body is not serving the useful purpose it should. That would be a natural conclusion. However, I feel that a certain responsibility rests with the United Nations assembly. I definitely feel this matter should be high on the agenda of the United Nations discussions because, Mr. Speaker, again I say there is no greater problem that faces us, next to the battle against aggression, than the battle against famine and hunger.
This is a matter that deeply concerns us all. The facts are that before world war II there was enough food being produced to provide every man, woman and child with 2,380 calories per day. After twelve years of so-called progress we have enough food to supply every man, woman and child with 2,260 calories per day, 120 calories less than we had twelve years ago. We can therefore understand the reason that the food and agriculture organization recommends an increased demand for food. Again I say this problem should rest with the United Nations assembly itself.
The speech from the throne made no reference to the position of agriculture. I believe that was an important and very serious omission on the part of the government. I feel that agriculture in Canada today is in a most difficult position, regardless of the statements by the previous speaker. In my view the present position of the farmer is certainly not bright.
I have just come from the farm to attend this session of parliament, and many of our members have some knowledge of the situation. It is really very serious indeed. The farmers have seen labour ask for and receive higher remuneration for their services; they have seen the prices of the goods that they

The Address-Mr. Catherwood have to purchase rising higher and higher. On the other hand they see the prices of pork and beef tumbling. They see a lessening in the demand for poultry products, and dairy prices are levelling off. These, gentlemen, are not very nice things to have to bring before the house. We would like to say that conditions are bright and cheerful, but such is not the case.
A real challenge faces us in this House of Commons, as we meet to discuss and debate these problems. Agriculture today is fast approaching a crisis. Whatever is done about the farm situation at the present session of parliament is going to be very important to the primary producers of this country. We trust that legislation will be brought forth which will improve the position of the farmers of Canada. We, as Canadian citizens, owe so much to our farm people. When that industry is kept in a strong, healthy condition, it means that Canada's economy is healthy. It is to be hoped the government will make a definite statement of policy as to what they have in view, particularly with regard to regaining our markets.
We know that on many occasions we have pressed for a commonwealth conference. We know that our leader has repeatedly suggested such a conference. As farmers we realize what such a meeting means. It means a great deal to us. We trust that the commonwealth meeting which is now being held, and which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is attending, will result in something of value to the agricultural industry of Canada. I hope that, along with what I have suggested, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the members of the government will take into very serious consideration the fact that this matter of trade is so important to the farm people of Canada.
